newsitem.title: USA: Mexico grain/oilseed imports seen rising by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Mexico grain/oilseed imports seen rising by 2000.

text.p: Mexico will be importing about 10 million tonnes of grains and oilseeds annually by the year 2000, most of which will come from the United States, the leader of a Mexican farm organisation said.

Speaking Monday at the American Farm Bureau Federation convention here, Miguel Castro Sanchez, president of Consejo Nacional Agropecuario, said Mexico will import about six million tonnes of grains and oilseeds in 1997 and that amount should increase 10 to 12 percent annually until 2000.
Canola should come from Canada while the balance will be from the United States.
"They (Mexico) are not really interested in importing grain from Argentina," he said through a translator.
About half of the 10 million tonnes will be corn, a quarter of it soybeans and the balance sorghum, wheat and canola. These imports will be processed into food or poultry and hog feed.
Castro said Mexican farmers will not be able to keep pace with rising domestic food demand, plus many farmers are not efficient enough to compete with imports.
"Farmers in Mexico need to understand if they cannot be competitive they need to get into other crops," he said, suggesting fruits, lumber, or hay.

Sanchez' remarks came during a convention session reviewing the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), which he said was responsible for increasing Mexico's agricultural exports to the U.S. by nearly 49 percent from 1993 to 1996.
"Today we are seeing avocadoes, hog meat and fruits...entering the North American markets," he said.
